title: Orphan entity remediation notebook
content:
Purpose and context:
This is a working scratchpad for addressing the "orphan entity" problem in the current NER/labeling pipeline: short entity spans that are isolated, ambiguous, or lack canonical mapping (e.g., "Zyph", "J-1203-1") and therefore get dropped or misrouted in downstream models and QA. Note: this is intentionally rough — meant to capture heuristics, sample cases, quick regex ideas, and a lightweight remediation plan we can hand off to SRE/engineering for automation experiments.

High-level goal:
- Reduce orphaned/unknown-entity drop rate by 60% on priority datasets (user-chat logs + support tickets) without significantly increasing false positives.
- Provide clear micro-rules for annotators so that manual curation is consistent.

Quick definitions (for this doc):
- orphan entity: a labeled span with no canonical match in our entity index and insufficient context to confidently map (e.g., "Zyph", "J-1203-1").
- weak span: very short spans (1–3 chars) or punctuation-heavy tokens often mis-tagged as entities (e.g., "@", "#1").
- fragment: entity-like substring of a larger token (e.g., "corp" inside "autocorp-42").

Top observed failure modes (examples):
1) Truncated names from tokenization: "Michae" (was originally "Michael") — appears in chat snippet after cropping.
   - Impact: lost identity mapping, downstream user history linking fails.
2) IDs with multiple formats: "inv-00123" vs "INV00123" vs "00123" — canonicalization missing.
   - Impact: dedupe and billing joins break.
3) Cross-lingual fragments: "Banco" appears in Spanish logs but matched to English bank names incorrectly.
4) Punctuation-only artifacts: "#", "--", "..." captured as entity span when annotator tool boundary heuristics are off.
5) Compound tokens concatenated by OCR or copy/paste: "AcmeInc2021Report" should have been "Acme Inc 2021 Report".

Annotation heuristics (draft) — rules annotators can apply quickly:
- Minimum character rule: if span length < 2 characters, mark as "needs_review" unless strong contextual indicator (phone country code like "+1").
- ID normalization: strip non-alphanumeric and compare case-insensitive; require at least 3 digits/letters to auto-map.
- Hyphen/underscore splitting: if token contains hyphen/underscore and the resulting parts match known entities, prefer split.
- OCR concatenation detection: long token with mixed alpha+digit length > 12 and camelcase or digit clusters -> suggest splitting.
- Language signal: if document language != en and span is common foreign term (list TBD), prefer non-mapping until manual review.

Sample problematic rows (copy these into small batch for annotators):
- "chat": "hey i sent invoice INV-00123 but status says unknown"  -> span: "INV-00123"  -> suggested: normalize to "INV00123"; map to invoice table if > 4 digits.
- "ticket": "client: Banco Surfiia" -> span: "Banco Surfiia" -> fuzzy candidate: "Banco Surfinia" (confidence 0.62) -> mark for review.
- "message": "Transferred to acmeinc2021report via sftp" -> span: "acmeinc2021report" -> recommend splitting to [Acme Inc, 2021, report].
- "note": "tried calling +1 415-" -> span: "+1" -> needs_review (insufficient digits).

Heuristic patterns / regex ideas (fast experiments):
- ID canonicalizer: s/[^A-Za-z0-9]+//g  (strip non-alphanum) then toUpperCase -> compare. Reject if length < 4.
- CamelCase splitter: s/(?<=[a-z])(?=[A-Z])|(?<=[A-Za-z])(?=\d)/ /g -> crude token split.
- OCR noise filter: if token has > 60% repetition of one char or punctuation, mark as noise.

Automation experiments to try (high ROI small tasks):
1) Preprocessing hook that normalizes common ID patterns before NER (apply regex canonicalizer).
2) Fuzzy-candidate matcher against entity index using edit distance threshold that varies by token length.
3) Tiny language-detector pass to bias mapping rules for non-en content.
4) Post-annotation filter that flags 1–2 char spans for queueing to "quick human review" rather than auto-drop.

Micro-batch review checklist for annotators (5–7 min per batch):
- Validate that each flagged orphan has: (a) original context sentence, (b) tokenized form, (c) suggested canonical form or reason for keep/remove.
- If mapping is likely but fuzzy, add candidate canonical and note confidence.
- If unsure, mark "needs_review" and add 1–2 words explaining uncertainty.

Edge-case decision examples (I keep revising these; copy into annotation guide):
- "J-1203-1" vs "J12031": prefer canonical without separators if digits >= 5.
- Tokens starting with '#' followed by digits: if in a support ticket, treat as internal ref and attempt map; otherwise drop.
- Single-letter spans followed by punctuation: keep only if attached to an acronym list (doc-level).

Prioritization and sampling plan:
- Priority datasets: recent support tickets (last 90 days), closed-chat transcripts with payment mentions, and onboarding flows.
- Sampling rule: sample 1% of total dataset but oversample documents with > 3 orphan candidates.

Manual remediation plan (short):
- Phase 1 (manual curation): 2 annotators, 2 days -> curate 2k orphan candidates, produce consolidated canonical mapping rules and 200 gold examples.
- Phase 2 (automate & validate): implement ID canonicalizer and fuzzy matcher; run on a 10k holdout and compute precision/recall against gold.
- Phase 3 (rollout): integrate into preprocessing pipeline and route low-confidence cases to human-in-the-loop.

Open questions / TODOs (tickets / owners):
- Q1: What is the canonical threshold for fuzzy map by length? (owner: @Priya; JIRA-ML-847)
- Q2: Should we maintain an "entity alias" table in the service or rely on on-the-fly fuzzy matches? Pros/cons doc needed. (owner: @Ethan)
- Q3: Are there privacy implications for storing raw IDs from tickets? Check with legal. (owner: @Riley; ask Legal)

Notes-to-self:
- Pull existing alias list from CONFLUENCE-entity-guidelines-v2 and dedupe with script in linked PR.
- Build a tiny dashboard to surface top 100 orphan tokens by frequency — will make manual curation faster.

Next immediate steps (this sprint):
1) Create 2k micro-batch in Label Studio with the sample rows above + 1k random orphans (owner: Riley).
2) Draft a short annotator cheat-sheet (1 page) with the heuristics and share with labeling crew.
3) Spike canonicalizer in Python (strip, upcase, length filter) and run locally on 10k messages.

Last thought: keep the rules conservative — better to route to quick human review than to create noisy mappings that corrupt downstream joins. This doc will morph into the handoff for engineering and the first iteration of the alias table.
